title: CLO 2025.0 - Keyframe Animation
description: CLO 2025.0 version has been officially released — intelligent, powerful, and endlessly creative! Create more dynamic and exciting content using keyframe animation.
transcript:
In this video, I will introduce you to the keyframe animation function.  
In version 2025.0, keyframes can be applied to various elements such as colors, fabrics, panels, joints, fixed pins, and wind control devices to achieve natural transition animations at any time.  
The original animation mode was changed to the animation editor after this update, making it convenient for everyone to create animations directly in simulation mode.  
Overall usability has also been improved.  

Click on "Animation" in the top menu, then select "Animation Editor" to open it.  
First, let's look at the animation editor layout after the update and see how to set up keyframes.  
You can see that the toolbar at the top of the editor retains familiar options such as recording, playback, camera animation, and simulation quality.  
In addition, the automatic keyframe function has been added, and other configuration-related settings have been moved to the configuration panel on the right.  

On the left side of the editor, the animation layer list is set as a tree structure, displaying animation objects in the scene.  
When applying animation, costumes, wind controllers, and flags will appear as object layers at the top level.  
Click the triangle next to each object to check the animatable properties.  
These properties will be displayed as property layers.  

The name of the object layer cannot be edited directly in the animation editor, but for some objects, you can rename them in the object window scene selection tab.  
To set up a keyframe, click on the right side of the property layer to insert a keyframe.  
Depending on the different properties, you can use the option box to enable or disable the property or enter a specific value to manually set the keyframe.  
Keyframes will be displayed as zero-shaped icons, making them easy to identify.  

The animation track in the middle of the screen adjusts to display the animation range of each object, helping you clearly control animation timing and space.  
Animations based on simulation storage, such as costume or software model animations, will be displayed in red, while keyframe animations will be displayed in gray.  

Click the animation button on the top left to open a list of objects that support animation, including colors, materials, panels, virtual models, and cameras.  
After selecting an object, it will be added to the object list, and you can apply keyframes to it.  

Next, let’s look at the timeline area in the middle of the interface.  
The curve line above the gray bar at the top indicates the playback range.  
It defines the part of the animation that will be played.  
You can adjust the playback range in the following ways:  
- Drag both ends: directly drag the two ends of the gray bar.  
- Drag the entire timeline: press the mouse button and drag the gray bar to move the playback range.  

The keyframe and end frame adjustments will also be reflected in the configuration panel.  
You can also enter values directly in the configuration panel to set them.  
Click the right arrow on the timeline to choose to set the start or end frame and set the current frame as the start or end point of the playback range.  
Choosing to limit the range to the action frames will automatically adjust the playback range to include all existing keyframes.  

Additionally, you can press the Ctrl key and scroll the mouse wheel to zoom in or out on the timeline, allowing you to check the keyframe range more precisely.  
The timeline slider at the bottom allows you to set the keyframe range.  
Click the right arrow in the slider area to reveal three options:  
- Configure action frames: the timeline will automatically adjust to all animation layers and the range between the first and last keyframe in the animation layers.  
- Configure playback range: adjusts the preview according to the currently defined playback range.  
- Configure all frames: adjusts the preview according to the current timeline with the smallest and largest keyframes set at both ends of the slider.  

You can also directly click the button on the right side of the end frame input box to complete this operation.  

The configuration panel on the right allows you to control some general playback settings, such as timeline range, scene time curve, and display units.  
Two new options have been added: Real Time and Save Time.  

Real Time, often referred to as FPS, defines the playback rate per second.  
The higher the real time, the smoother the animation playback, but it also increases rendering time and file size.  
You can choose the appropriate real time according to your project needs to balance quality and performance.  

Save Time controls how keyframes behave when changing the real time.  
- When this option is off, the total playback time remains unchanged, but the keyframes’ real time will be adjusted according to the new FPS.  
- When this option is on, the keyframes’ real time remains unchanged, and the total playback time adjusts according to the new FPS.  

These new functions allow you to more flexibly control the animation playback range and speed, optimizing your workflow.  

Now, let’s learn how to create and edit animations.  
For saving animation based on simulation, such as clothing or software models, you can continue using the record button as before.  

In version 2025, we added the functions of cutting and merging animation layers.  
Previously, editing and recording good animation layers often required third-party software.  
Now, you can freely cut or merge layers as needed.  

To cut a layer, right-click on the layer you want to cut, then select "Cut Layer."  
The layer will be cut at the current real time, and the segment will appear directly in the track above the original layer.  

To merge multiple layers, press the Ctrl key and select the layers to merge, or use the Shift key to select continuously, then right-click and select "Merge Layers."  
When merging layers, the topmost layer is used as the standard.  
Since the current animation layers are cut and received, the effect between them naturally continues.  
If there is overlap, higher-level data takes priority during merging.  

You can also play and check the effect before merging layers to ensure consistency.  
After confirming the effect, you can perform the merge operation.  

For file-stored animations, which differ from objects listed in the animation menu, manual keyframe setting is required for the animation to work.  

Let’s look at each animation project and review how to set keyframes and other important notes.  

We will start with color animation.  
There are two ways to set keyframes:  
- Use the add animation button in the layer table.  
- Set directly from the editor or attribute editor of the object.  

Click the add animation button and select "Color."  
Create an empty flag layer, then click the triangle on the left to open the layer and check its properties.  
In the drop-down menu, you can see the flag list usable for clothing.  
The flag list content updates in real time according to the flags in the flag editor.  

Now, first add a keyframe for the white flag.  
The first keyframe will appear on the first frame in the hidden layer.  
The keyframe is based on the setting of the current frame.  
You can directly move the playhead to the target frame, select the flag color, and click to insert the keyframe.  
Alternatively, enter the frame number in the current frame input box, select the flag color, and click to insert the keyframe.  

To check whether the keyframe has been added correctly, use the arrow buttons on the left and right sides of the keyframe to quickly jump between existing keyframes.  
After confirming the keyframe is in place, return to the first frame and click the play button.  
You will see the flag color transition smoothly, presenting a natural animation effect through the set keyframes.  

Now, let’s see how to add a keyframe directly from the flag editor.  
Move to the position where you want to add the keyframe, select a flag color, and then click to insert the keyframe in the upper right corner of the editor.  
After adding the keyframe, you can drag the two ends of the object layer to adjust the overall length while maintaining the relative distance between them.  
You can also drag the entire layer to move all keyframes at once or press and drag each keyframe to a new position to adjust its placement.  
Select multiple keyframes together by clicking or pressing Shift, then move them as a group to keep their relative positions.  

To delete specific keyframes, press and drag to select multiple keyframes, then right-click and select "Delete Keyframe," or press the Delete key on the keyboard.  

If too many animation layers slow down playback, click the eye icon on the left side to enable or disable playback of individual animations.  
Try playing it to see the current speed.  

Now, cut back to the first frame and turn off the flag color animation.  
You will see that after turning off the flag color animation layer, the playback speed is noticeably faster.  

If you want to delete an animation layer, right-click the layer in the list and select "Delete Layer."  
Since the layer uses a tree structure, deleting an object layer will also delete related attribute layers.  
If you accidentally delete an attribute layer, right-click the object layer and select "Add Layer" to re-add it.  
You will see a list of movable attributes and can choose which attributes to add separately.  

Now, let’s see how to create a virtual model animation, including using joint points to adjust posture and set keyframes.  
Click the "Add Animation" button.  
The mouse will stop on the virtual model list, showing virtual models added in the current scene.  
Click the required virtual model to add it to the layer list.  
Click the triangle to open and check its attribute layers.  

To add the current position as the first keyframe, set the current frame to 0 first, then click the keyframe button on the right to set the keyframe.  

Press Shift + X on the keyboard to display the virtual model's joint points in the 3D window.  
Next, move the playback head, change the pin position, adjust the joint points to modify the posture, then click the keyframe button on the right side of the joint layer to insert a keyframe.  
Set another keyframe.  

Because virtual model animation usually needs to be repeated with steps of moving pins, adjusting positions, and inserting keyframes, the automatic keyframe function is more efficient.  
You can insert the keyframe manually on the first frame, then enable automatic keyframe.  
In this way, any subsequent joint adjustments will automatically generate keyframes.  
If a pin already has a keyframe, the new position will overwrite the existing keyframe.  

Now the virtual model's posture is roughly edited.  
Cut back to the first frame to confirm the animation effect.  

After confirming the current effect, you can copy and paste keyframes.  
Click or drag to select one or more keyframes, right-click and select "Copy Keyframe," or press Ctrl + C.  
Move the playback head to the frame where you want to paste, right-click and select "Paste Keyframe," or press Ctrl + V.  
The keyframe will be pasted on the current frame.  
If you paste multiple keyframes, it will keep their original frame positions.  

Now, play the animation again to check the effect after pasting the keyframes.  

You can also right-click the object layer and use the context menu to adjust joint pins and move them to the ground.  

Additionally, you can download and modify existing MTN files, but to avoid remodeling in the current scene, please open the file in a new window.  

Now, let’s see how to set animation for panels by adding keyframes.  
You can control material changes on selected panels at any time.  

To create animation, after selecting the panel, increase the animation by pressing the animation button.  
However, for panels, it is usually more efficient to insert keyframes directly from the property editor.  

First, set the position where the keyframe needs to be added (this position is set as the current frame).  
Then select the panel with the animation effect to be added.  
In the property editor, select the material for the panel to be used, then click the keyframe button next to the material.  
This will automatically add the panel to the layer table and insert a fabric keyframe at the current frame.  

Move the playhead to another frame.  
At this time, you can also enable automatic keyframe to reduce operations.  
Change the fabric in the property editor.  
You can repeat this process as needed.  

When playing the animation, you will see the fabric of the selected panel change over time.  

Now, let’s see how to set animation for fabric properties.  
You can set keyframes for the fabric properties and physical properties separately.  

Click the add animation button, then select the fabric to animate.  
The selected fabric will be added to the layer table as an object layer.  
Click the triangle to open it and see the property layers automatically listed below.  

These property layers include some PBR properties and physical properties.  
If the front and back sides of the fabric use different textures, you can set keyframes for each surface property separately.  

If you want to add only specific properties to the layer table, select the fabric in the object window, then set keyframes in the usual way: set the current frame, adjust the value, then click to insert the keyframe.  

Because automatic keyframe is enabled here, you only need to modify the corresponding property parameters to add keyframes to the current frame.  

Please remember that pattern, fabric, and color animations all control properties related to fabric.  
If you change these three types of animation applied to the same piece of clothing, their interaction may lead to unexpected results.  
Therefore, it is recommended to separate pattern or fabric animation from color animation.  

Next, let’s see how to set animation for simulation properties.  
Click the add animation button, then select simulation properties.  
An object layer will be added to the layer table, but no property layers will be displayed by default.  

To display property layers, right-click and select simulation properties in the 3D window or click the simulation property layer in the list.  
The preview will change to custom, allowing you to set keyframes for gravity and air resistance.  

Next, I will introduce how to set fixed pin animation.  
Fixed pin animation allows you to set keyframes for the activation or deactivation state of fixed pins.  

First, add a fixed pin in the 3D window, then use the add animation button to add the fixed pin object to the layer table.  

Note that the default names of fixed pins and wind controllers are the same when created.  
Therefore, it is recommended to add a fixed pin, select it, and rename it in the property editor.  
This way, you can quickly select the fixed pin you want to edit.  

To control the transition between keyframes and adjust animation speed, you can set transition effects.  

To change the transition effect, select the keyframe you want, right-click it, then select the transition effect from the menu.  

- The long-term transition effect maintains the current transition effect unchanged until the next keyframe switches to the corresponding effect.  
- The linear transition effect connects different keyframes with straight lines to create smooth, stable transitions.  
- The cubic transition effect connects keyframes with curved lines to achieve more dynamic transitions.  
This function is especially effective when using three or more keyframes, as the transition looks more natural.  

According to the attribute type selected by the keyframe in the layer, only supported transition effects appear in the menu.  
Changing the transition effect of one keyframe will automatically apply the same type to all keyframes in the same position below.  

Finally, click the cancel stop button to separate the animation editor window into an independent window.  
After canceling the stop, you can click full screen to expand the editor to full screen.  

In dual-display settings, you can use the editor on a separate screen to improve workflow.  
To restore the original window size, click the restore button.  
To restart the editor to the main interface, click the stop button.  

This concludes the introduction to keyframe animation.  
Because wind controller and camera animation follow the same workflow, detailed introduction is not necessary here.  
For more detailed information, please refer to the user manual.  

I hope you use your imagination and take advantage of the new functions in the animation editor to create dynamic and wonderful content.  
Thank you for watching.

chunks.title: CLO 2025.0 - Keyframe Animation
chunks.content: # CLO 2025.0 - Keyframe Animation This document explains the keyframe animation features in CLO 2025.0, detailing how to apply and manage animations for colors, fabrics, panels, joints, fixed pins, and wind controllers. It covers the new animation editor interface, keyframe setup, timeline controls, animation layer management, and specific animation workflows. --- ## Animation Editor Overview and Layout This section describes the updated animation editor interface in CLO 2025.0, including how to access it, the layout of toolbars, animation layers, and keyframe controls. - Access the animation editor via **Animation > Animation Editor** in the top menu. - The editor includes a familiar toolbar with options for recording, playback, camera animation, and simulation quality. - A new **automatic keyframe function** has been added. - The right side contains the **configuration panel** for playback and animation settings. - The left side shows the **animation layer list** structured as a tree with object layers at the top level (costumes, wind controllers, flags). - Expanding an object layer reveals **property layers** showing animatable properties. - Object layer names cannot be edited directly in the editor but can be renamed in the object window scene selection tab. - Keyframes are inserted by clicking on the right side of a property layer; they appear as zero-shaped icons. - The central **animation track** displays animation ranges and timing, distinguishing simulation-based animations (red) from keyframe animations (gray). - The animation button at the top left opens a list of animatable objects including colors, materials, panels, virtual models, and cameras for adding to the layer list. --- ## Timeline Controls and Playback Range This section explains timeline manipulation for controlling animation playback, setting keyframe ranges, and zooming. - The **curve line** above the gray timeline bar indicates playback range. - Adjust playback range by dragging the ends of the gray bar or dragging the entire bar. - Start and end frames can be set via the timeline right arrow menu or configuration panel. - The option to **limit range to action frames** automatically adjusts the playback range to include all keyframes. - Zoom timeline view with **Ctrl + mouse wheel**. - The timeline slider area offers three configuration options: - **Configure action frames**: adjusts range to first and last keyframes across all layers. - **Configure playback range**: previews the defined playback range. - **Configure all frames**: previews the timeline from smallest to largest keyframe. - The configuration panel allows setting timeline range, scene time curve, and display units. - New options include: - **Real Time (FPS)**: controls playback frame rate; higher FPS improves smoothness but increases rendering time and file size. - **Save Time**: toggles how keyframes behave when FPS changes: - Off: total playback time is fixed; keyframe real time adjusts. - On: keyframe real time is fixed; total playback time adjusts. --- ## Creating and Editing Animations This section covers how to create, cut, merge, and manage animation layers and keyframes. - For simulation-based animations (e.g., clothing), continue using the record button.

chunks.title: CLO 2025.0 - Keyframe Animation
chunks.content: - Enable **automatic keyframe** after the first manual insertion to auto-generate keyframes on joint adjustments. - New keyframes overwrite existing ones for the same pin. - Copy and paste keyframes using Ctrl + C/V or right-click context menu; pasted keyframes retain original frame positions. - Joint pins can be adjusted or moved to the ground via the object layer menu. - Existing MTN files can be downloaded and modified; to avoid modifying the current scene, open MTN files in a new window. --- ## Panel Animation This section covers animating panels by keyframing material changes. - Select a panel and add animation via the animation button. - More efficient to insert keyframes directly from the panel's property editor. - Set the current frame, select the panel, choose a material, and click the keyframe button next to the material. - The panel and fabric keyframe will be added to the layer table automatically. - Move the playhead to another frame, enable automatic keyframe, change the fabric, and repeat as needed. - Playback shows fabric changes over time on the selected panel. --- ## Fabric Animation This section explains animating fabric properties, including physical and PBR attributes. - Add fabric animation from the **Add Animation** button. - The fabric is added as an object layer with property layers for different attributes. - Separate keyframes can be set for front and back side textures. - To add specific properties, select the fabric in the object window, set the current frame, adjust values, and insert keyframes. - Automatic keyframe mode allows keyframe creation by simply modifying property values. - **Important:** Pattern, fabric, and color animations all affect fabric properties. Applying these simultaneously to the same clothing may cause unexpected interactions. It is recommended to separate pattern/fabric animations from color animations. --- ## Simulation Property Animation This section describes animating simulation properties like gravity and air resistance. - Add simulation property animation via **Add Animation**. - The object layer is added without property layers by default. - Right-click the simulation property layer or 3D window to display property layers. - Switch preview to custom mode to set keyframes for gravity, air resistance, and other simulation parameters. --- ## Fixed Pin Animation This section details animating fixed pins by controlling their activation states. - Add fixed pins in the 3D window. - Add fixed pin objects to the layer table with the **Add Animation** button. - Default fixed pin and wind controller names are identical upon creation; rename pins in the property editor for easier selection. - Insert keyframes to toggle activation or deactivation states. --- ## Transition Effects Between Keyframes This section explains how to control animation speed and interpolation between keyframes. - Change transition effects by right-clicking a keyframe and selecting from: - **Long-term transition**: maintains current transition until the next keyframe. - **Linear transition**: connects keyframes with straight lines for smooth, stable changes. - **Cubic transition**: uses curved lines for dynamic, natural transitions, effective with three or more keyframes.

rename pins in the property editor for easier selection. - Insert keyframes to toggle activation or deactivation states. --- ## Transition Effects Between Keyframes This section explains how to control animation speed and interpolation between keyframes. - Change transition effects by right-clicking a keyframe and selecting from: - **Long-term transition**: maintains current transition until the next keyframe. - **Linear transition**: connects keyframes with straight lines for smooth, stable changes. - **Cubic transition**: uses curved lines for dynamic, natural transitions, effective with three or more keyframes. - Only transition effects supported by the selected keyframe’s attribute appear. - Changing one keyframe’s transition effect applies the same type to all keyframes in the same position below. --- ## Animation Editor Window Management This section outlines window controls and multi-display workflow improvements. - Click the **Cancel Stop** button to detach the animation editor into an independent window. - Full screen mode expands the editor for better visibility. - In dual-monitor setups, use the detached editor on a separate screen to enhance workflow. - Restore the original window size with the **Restore** button. - Return the editor to the main interface with the **Stop** button. --- ## Additional Notes - Wind controller and camera animations follow the same workflow and are not detailed here. - For more detailed instructions, refer to the official user manual. --- This guide provides comprehensive instructions for utilizing CLO 2025.0's keyframe animation features to create detailed and dynamic garment animations, enhancing simulation realism and creative control.
